book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Eight Essentials for Professional Options Trading
body: Bittman identifies eight topics every advanced trader must master: (1) option market fundamentals, (2) option price behavior including the Greeks, (3) synthetic relationships, (4) pricing arbitrage strategies, (5) volatility, (6) delta-neutral trading, (7) pricing arbitrage using bid-ask spreads, (8) managing position risk. Mastering all eight separates a professional trader from a retail speculator.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Seven-Part Option Trade Instruction
body: Unlike a four-part stock order (action, quantity, name, price), an option order requires seven decisions: (1) action (buy-to-open, sell-to-close, etc.), (2) quantity (contracts), (3) underlying, (4) expiration month, (5) strike price, (6) option type (call or put), (7) price per share. Each additional dimension means more ways a position can gain or lose value.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Call vs. Put: Rights and Obligations
body: Call: gives the owner the right to buy the underlying at the strike price; gives the writer the obligation to sell. Put: gives the owner the right to sell the underlying at the strike price; gives the writer the obligation to buy. All four parties — call buyer, call seller, put buyer, put seller — have distinct P/L profiles and risk characteristics.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: In-the-Money, At-the-Money, Out-of-the-Money
body: Call ITM when stock > strike; ATM when stock ≈ strike; OTM when stock < strike. Put ITM when stock < strike; ATM when stock ≈ strike; OTM when stock > strike. ITM options have intrinsic value (stock-price difference vs. strike). ATM and OTM options have only time value. Traders commonly call an option 'at the money' even when the stock is near — but not exactly at — the strike.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Intrinsic Value vs. Time Value
body: Option price = intrinsic value + time value. Intrinsic value is the in-the-money amount (max 0 vs. stock-strike difference). Time value is the remainder. Deep-ITM options trade near intrinsic value with minimal time premium; a 55 Call with stock at 67 has intrinsic value of 12 and zero time value — it 'trades at parity.' OTM options consist entirely of time value.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Public Traders vs. Market Makers: Role and Priority
body: Public traders are individuals and institutions without exchange membership. Market makers are exchange members who quote both bids and offers, providing liquidity. Market makers earn the bid-ask spread for their liquidity provision. Exchanges may accept public orders before market maker orders at the same price (customer priority), but market makers can trade ahead at better prices.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Margin Requirements and Maintenance Margin
body: Initial margin: minimum equity required to open a marginable position (e.g., 50% for stock purchases). Maintenance margin: minimum equity required to keep the position open (lower than initial, e.g., 25%). A margin call occurs when account equity falls below maintenance margin — broker requires deposit or liquidation. Option sellers face margin requirements because of potential assignment obligations.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Short Stock Rebate: Income for Professional Traders
body: When professional traders short stock, they receive a rebate on the interest generated by the short sale proceeds. Market makers typically receive 80% of net interest from short stock positions. This rebate affects arbitrage pricing: it reduces the carrying cost of short-stock positions, making conversions and reverse conversions more profitable and tightening the pricing boundaries.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: P/L Diagrams: Long and Short Calls
body: Long call P/L diagram: hockey-stick at expiration — loss limited to premium paid below break-even; profit unlimited above. Three curves shown (expiration, 60 days, 30 days prior) reveal time premium. Short call: inverted hockey-stick — max profit is premium received; unlimited loss above break-even. Curved prior-to-expiry lines show why short options have positive theta but dangerous gamma.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: P/L Diagrams: Long and Short Puts
body: Long put: profit rises as stock falls below break-even; loss limited to premium above break-even. Short put: premium received above break-even; increasing loss below. Both strategies show three time curves. Unlike calls, put time-value behavior is symmetric on the downside. Short puts are commonly used to generate income in range-bound or mildly bullish markets.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Long Straddle vs. Short Straddle: When Each Wins
body: Long straddle (long call + long put same strike/expiry): profits from large moves in either direction; loses the full premium if stock stays at the strike. Short straddle (short call + short put): max profit at the strike; unlimited losses in both directions. Long straddle requires a 'big' move either way; short straddle profits from calm, range-bound price action and high IV crushing to lower realized vol.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Strangles vs. Straddles: Key Differences
body: Strangle: different strike prices for call and put (e.g., 95 Put + 105 Call). Wider break-even points but cheaper than a straddle. Straddle has higher premium (both options ATM) and narrower break-even but greater probability of profit. Long strangle needs a bigger move to profit; short strangle has a wider profit zone. For given stock, straddle > strangle in premium but straddle expires worthless less often.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Vertical Spreads: Bull Call and Bear Call
body: Long vertical call spread (bull call): buy lower-strike call, sell higher-strike call. Limited profit (spread width minus net debit); limited risk (net debit). Short vertical call spread (bear call): sell lower-strike call, buy higher-strike call. Net credit received; profit below lower strike, loss above higher strike. Both have defined risk and reward — the primary advantage over naked calls.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Butterfly and Condor Spreads: Four-Leg Defined Risk
body: Long butterfly (calls): buy lower strike, sell 2 middle strikes, buy upper strike. Max profit at middle strike; limited loss at extremes. Long condor (calls): buy lowest, sell next two, buy highest. Flat profit plateau between inner strikes; limited loss outside. Both profit from low realized volatility keeping stock near the center. Condor is wider but requires more premium. Both are 'short vol' at the center.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Op-Eval Pro: Single Option Calculator
body: The book uses Op-Eval Pro software to illustrate option pricing. The Single Option Calculator inputs: stock price, strike, volatility, interest rate, dividends, days to ex-div, days to expiry. Outputs: theoretical call and put values, delta, gamma, vega, 7-theta, rho. Example: stock 58, strike 60, vol 35%, int 4% → call value 46.73, delta 0.93, vega 0.40.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Theoretical Price Table: Time and Moneyness Matrix
body: A theoretical price table shows option values at a matrix of stock prices (rows) and days to expiry (columns). Example: 100 Call at 20% vol. Reading down a column: ITM options worth more than OTM. Reading across a row: option value decreases as time passes (time decay). At-the-money at 60 days ~$2; at 6 days ~$0.44. Table provides quick reference for strategy evaluation without recalculating.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Option Price Behavior: Two Distinct Aspects
body: Option price behavior requires mastering two distinct aspects: (1) how prices change as market conditions change (stock price, time, volatility, interest rates, dividends) — covered in Chapter 3; (2) how the Greeks measure these sensitivities and how they change as conditions change — covered in Chapter 4. A trader who understands only one aspect will be surprised by positions.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Options as Insurance: The Four Pricing Components
body: Options are priced like insurance policies. Four pricing components: (1) stock price (the asset being insured); (2) strike price (the coverage level); (3) time to expiration (coverage period); (4) volatility (the risk factor — analogous to driving record). Additionally: interest rates and dividends affect pricing. Higher volatility → higher option prices, just as riskier drivers pay more insurance.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Interest Rates and Dividends: Opposite Effects on Calls vs. Puts
body: Interest rates and dividends have opposite effects: higher interest rates → call prices rise, put prices fall (cost of carry). Higher dividends → call prices fall, put prices rise (dividend reduces stock on ex-date). These effects are significant for LEAPS and for positions held through ex-dividend dates. They are the mechanical basis of rho and the reason deep-ITM calls may be exercised early.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Call Values and Stock Price: Positive Correlation with Delta
body: Call values are positively correlated with stock prices: as stock rises, call value rises. The relationship is not linear — it is curved (convex). Delta measures the slope: when stock is $86 and call is far OTM, delta ≈ 0.05 (barely moves). As stock reaches $100 (ATM), delta ≈ 0.55. At $114 (deep ITM), delta approaches 1.00. This convexity (gamma) means call values accelerate faster than delta alone predicts on sharp moves.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Delta: Introduction and Initial Definition
body: Delta is introduced as the ratio of option price change to stock price change. If a 100 Call rises from 6.53 to 7.11 when the stock rises from $100 to $101, the delta is 0.58 (call changed $0.58 per $1 stock move). Delta is not constant — it changes with stock price (captured by gamma). Delta also approximates the probability that the option will expire in the money.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Time Decay: Non-Linear Acceleration Near Expiration
body: Time decay is not linear. A 100 Call declines from 6.53 at 90 days to 5.92 at 75 days to 5.25 at 60 days — relatively slowly at first. Near expiration, the same $6.53 option might lose $2+ in the final two weeks. The curve is concave: each day costs more in dollar terms as expiration approaches. This acceleration is most pronounced for ATM options and is the basis of theta strategies.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Time Decay and Volatility: Higher Vol Slows OTM Decay Rate
body: Higher volatility slows the percentage decay of OTM options relative to ATM. A 110 Call at 20% vol declines 79% from 56 to 28 days, but only 21% in the final 28 days (most decay front-loaded). At 40% vol, the same 110 Call declines only 54% in the first half and 46% in the second — more even distribution. High-vol OTM options retain value longer. This affects roll timing for traders who sell OTM options.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Three-Part Forecast: Direction, Timing, and Volatility
body: Stock trading requires one forecast (direction). Option trading requires three simultaneous forecasts: (1) direction — will stock go up, down, or sideways? (2) timing — will it happen before expiration? (3) volatility — will IV rise or fall? Getting direction right but being wrong on timing or IV can result in a loss even on a correctly directional position. This three-dimensional decision framework is what distinguishes option traders from stock traders.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Multiple-Scenario Analysis for Option Strategies
body: Option traders must evaluate positions across multiple market scenarios — not just the most likely outcome. Scenario analysis means asking: what happens to the position if (A) the forecast is right and IV stays constant, (B) forecast is right but IV falls, (C) forecast is wrong but IV rises? Joe's analysis of Jumpco April 75 Calls illustrates this: each scenario produces different P/L, and only by examining all three does a trader understand what they are really buying or selling.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Index Options: European Exercise and Cash Settlement
body: Index options (SPX, NDX, etc.) typically stop trading on Thursday before the third Friday, with final settlement based on Friday morning opening prices. They are European-style (no early exercise). A call exercised when SPX is 20 points above strike delivers $2,000 in cash (20 × $100 multiplier). Settlement risk: the opening prices used for settlement can gap significantly from Thursday's closing prices.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Put Values and Stock Price: Inverse Correlation
body: Put values are inversely correlated with stock prices. A 100 Put rises as stock falls below the strike and approaches zero as stock rises far above. At expiration: put value = max(0, strike - stock). Before expiration, put retains time value even when stock is above the strike (OTM). The curve is mirror of the call curve but with a negative slope. Delta for puts is negative (-0.50 at the money, approaches -1.00 deep ITM).

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Chapter 4 — The Greeks: Overview
body: Five Greeks explain option price sensitivity: (1) Delta — stock price change. (2) Gamma — rate of delta change. (3) Vega — volatility change. (4) Theta — time decay. (5) Rho — interest rate change. Each Greek measures the impact of changing one input while all others remain constant. In the real world, multiple inputs change simultaneously, requiring traders to combine all Greek estimates.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Delta S-Curve: From 0 to 1 Across the Strike
body: Delta forms an S-curve as stock price changes. Deep OTM call delta ≈ 0; ATM ≈ 0.50; deep ITM ≈ 1.00. The S-shape means delta changes fastest near the strike (where gamma is highest). For puts: S-curve from 0 to -1.00. This characteristic means options become more sensitive to stock moves as they go further in the money — accelerating gains and losses. Traders monitor delta to understand their directional exposure.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Delta and Time: Minimal Effect Away from ATM
body: Time to expiry has little effect on delta for deep ITM or OTM options. A deep ITM 90 Call stays near delta 1.0 regardless of time. An OTM 110 Call stays near 0 regardless of time. Only ATM options (~0.50 delta) are relatively stable across time horizons. This means time alone doesn't dramatically shift directional exposure unless the option is at the money.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Delta and Volatility: High Vol Compresses Delta Toward 0.50
body: Higher volatility compresses all deltas toward 0.50. A deep ITM 90 Call delta falls from ~0.90 at low vol toward 0.50 at high vol. An OTM 110 Call delta rises from near 0 toward 0.50 at high vol. ATM stays at 0.50 regardless. Intuition: in a high-vol environment, any option has a reasonable chance of being anywhere at expiration — so all options approach 50/50 probability of expiring ITM.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Gamma Peak at ATM and Acceleration Near Expiration
body: Gamma is highest for ATM options and lowest for deep ITM/OTM. The gamma of an ATM option rises exponentially as expiration approaches — in the final 20 days, gamma can spike dramatically. An ATM 100 Call gamma rises from ~0.01 at 160 days to ~0.25+ near expiration. For ITM and OTM options, gamma remains low throughout. This is why short-gamma traders near expiry on ATM positions face amplified risk.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Gamma and Volatility: High Vol Reduces Gamma
body: Higher volatility reduces gamma for all options. As vol rises, the probability distribution of stock prices widens, making delta change more gradually per dollar move. A deep ITM call at low vol has high gamma (concentrated S-curve); at high vol, the S-curve is more gradual (lower gamma). Counterintuitive: even though high-vol options have large absolute moves, their delta changes per unit are smaller.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Vega: Highest for ATM Options and Long-Dated LEAPS
body: Vega is highest for ATM options and increases with time to expiry. A 100 Call has highest vega; a 90 Call or 110 Call has lower vega. Longer-dated options (LEAPS) have much more vega exposure than near-term options. This is why LEAPS are the preferred vehicle for volatility bets: a 1% rise in IV produces a larger dollar change than the same rise for a short-dated option.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Vega and Volatility: Concave Relationship
body: Vega is not constant across volatility levels. It rises from zero, peaks at moderate vol (~30–50%), then declines at extreme vol. Intuition: at very high vol, options are already nearly fully priced for uncertainty; additional vol increases add less and less marginal value. This means traders cannot assume a fixed dollar change per vol point — vega itself changes as IV moves.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Theta: ATM Options Lose the Most per Day
body: Theta (daily time decay) is most negative for ATM options. Deep ITM and OTM options have smaller absolute theta. The theta curve vs. stock price is an inverted bell shape peaking at the strike. As expiration approaches, ATM theta accelerates — the last few weeks of an ATM option's life see the most rapid dollar decay. This is the income source for short-option traders but the cost for long-option holders.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Theta Acceleration: Concave Decay Curve for ATM Options
body: An ATM 100 Call at 160 days has small theta (decays slowly). As expiration approaches, theta increases exponentially. The final 20 days may account for more time value erosion than the preceding 140 days. This concave decay curve means: (1) selling options in the last 3–6 weeks maximizes theta collection per unit of gamma risk; (2) buying ATM options far from expiry is expensive in theta but gives more time.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Theta and Volatility: Higher IV Increases Daily Decay
body: Higher implied volatility increases theta — options with more time premium decay faster in dollar terms. An ATM call at 50% IV has roughly 2.5x the theta of the same call at 20% IV. This confirms the gamma-theta linkage: the same conditions (high vol, ATM, near expiry) that maximize gamma also maximize theta. You cannot have one without the other.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Rho: Interest Rate Sensitivity — Calls Benefit, Puts Hurt
body: Rho measures sensitivity to interest rate changes. Call rho is positive (rising rates increase call value); put rho is negative (rising rates decrease put value). Rho is largest for long-dated, deep-ITM options (LEAPS). For short-dated OTM options, rho is nearly zero. Rho matters most for: LEAPS positions, arbitrage pricing of conversions and box spreads, and portfolios held for months to years.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Rho and Volatility: Higher Vol Reduces Rho
body: Rho decreases as volatility rises. At high vol, the intrinsic/carry component of option value is a smaller fraction of total value (time premium dominates). This makes rho less meaningful in high-IV environments. For practical trading: rho matters when rates change significantly or when pricing long-term positions. In short-dated, high-vol environments, rho is the least important Greek.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Position Delta: Scaling Option Delta to Full Position
body: Position delta = option delta × number of contracts × 100 shares. Example: long 4 XYZ 80 Calls, delta 0.55 → position delta = 4 × 0.55 × 100 = 220. This means the position behaves like being long 220 shares. A $1 stock rise produces approximately $220 gain. Position delta is the primary tool for understanding directional exposure and for calculating hedge ratios.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Position Gamma: How Delta Will Change on a Move
body: Position gamma = option gamma × contracts × 100. Example: long 4 XYZ 80 Calls, gamma 0.04 → position gamma = 0.16. If stock rises $1, position delta increases by 0.16 (from 2.20 to 2.36). For puts: long 10 QRS 40 Puts, gamma 0.11 → position gamma = 1.10. If stock rises $1, put delta moves from −3.40 to −2.40. Positive position gamma means you benefit from moves in both directions.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Position Vega: Dollar P/L from a 1% IV Change
body: Position vega = option vega × contracts × 100. Example: long 4 XYZ 80 Calls, vega 0.13 → position vega = 0.52. A 1% rise in IV increases position value by $52. For short options, position vega is negative — a 1% IV rise causes a loss. Position vega quantifies the exact dollar risk of being wrong on an IV direction bet. Short vega positions want IV to fall; long vega want IV to rise.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Position Theta: Daily Income or Cost in Dollars
body: Position theta = option theta × contracts × 100. Example: short 4 XYZ 80 Calls, theta 0.04 → position theta = +0.16, meaning the position gains $16 per day from time decay. For long 4 calls with same theta: position theta = −0.16 (costs $16/day). Theta is the daily P/L driver for option sellers. Over 30 days, short 4 calls at this theta generate $480 from time decay alone — assuming other factors constant.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Position Rho: Dollar P/L from a 1% Rate Change
body: Position rho = option rho × contracts × 100. Example: long 4 XYZ 80 Calls, rho 0.07 → position rho = +0.28. A 1% interest rate rise increases position value by $28. For short 10 QRS 40 Puts, rho −0.02 → position rho = −0.20: a 1% rate rise decreases position value by $20 (puts fall in value with rising rates, hurting short-put holder — less credit than expected). Rho scales with position size like all Greeks.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Negative Position Gamma: Delta Moves Against You
body: Short options have negative gamma. Example: short 10 QRS 40 Puts, gamma 0.11 → position gamma = −1.10. If stock rises $1: position delta changes from −3.40 to −2.40 (losing $100 delta exposure). On a stock drop, delta becomes more negative (position loses more rapidly). Negative gamma means the position's directional bias moves against the trader on any adverse move — losses compound.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Negative Position Vega: IV Rises Hurt Short-Option Positions
body: Short options have negative position vega. Example: short 4 XYZ 80 Calls, vega 0.13 → position vega = −0.52. A 1% IV rise causes a $52 loss on this position. In practice, IV often rises during adverse market moves (fear increases uncertainty), meaning short-option traders suffer doubly: from delta (directional loss) and from vega (IV expansion loss) simultaneously. This is the compounding risk of short vol.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Put-Call Parity: The Foundation of All Synthetics
body: Put-call parity: +Call − Put = +Stock. Rearranged: Long Stock = Long Call + Short Put (same strike, same expiry). All six basic positions (long/short stock, long/short call, long/short put) can be replicated by combining the other two instruments. This is not a theoretical curiosity — it is the structural relationship that: (1) underlies all arbitrage pricing, (2) determines which form of a position is cheapest, (3) enables market makers to hedge efficiently.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Synthetic Long Stock: Long Call + Short Put
body: Synthetic long stock = long call + short put (same strike, same expiry). P/L at any stock price equals the P/L of owning the actual stock. If interest rates and dividends are zero, this relationship is exact. In practice, the effective stock price of the synthetic depends on the net premium paid/received and the interest component. Used when: synthetics are more liquid than the stock, or to avoid margin requirements.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Synthetic Short Stock: Short Call + Long Put
body: Synthetic short stock = short call + long put (same strike, same expiry). Combined P/L matches short stock P/L. Used when: physically borrowing shares is expensive or unavailable, or to create short exposure in tax-advantaged accounts. Table 5-2 shows that at all stock prices, the combined position matches the short stock position's P/L exactly (before costs).

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Synthetic Long Call: Long Stock + Long Put
body: Synthetic long call = long stock + long put (same strike). The long put acts as downside protection; above the strike, position profits like a call. Cost = put premium paid. Example: long stock at $100 + long 100 Put at $3 = synthetic long call with effective premium of $3. Used when calls are unavailable or overpriced relative to puts + stock combination.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Synthetic Short Put: Covered Call
body: Short put = long stock + short call (covered call). The covered call position has exactly the same P/L at expiration as a naked short put. Both profit when stock stays at or above the short strike; both suffer the same dollar loss if stock falls below the break-even. This equivalence means: if you sell covered calls for income, you are synthetically short puts — with identical risk.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Effective Stock Price and the Time-Value Equality Rule
body: When interest rates are zero and there are no dividends, the time value of a call equals the time value of a put with the same strike. Example: stock at $97, strike $100 — Call value $3 (all time value), Put value $5.50 ($3 intrinsic + $2.50 time value — wait, put time value = $2.50 = call time value). In practice, with non-zero rates: call time value > put time value by the interest on the strike. Knowing this helps identify when one leg is relatively mispriced.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Interest Rate Effect on Synthetic Positions: Effective Stock Price
body: With non-zero interest rates, synthetics diverge slightly from real positions. A synthetic long call (long stock + long put) has an effective premium equal to the put premium plus interest on the stock price. If interest rates are 5% and the position is held for 30 days, the effective cost includes ~1/12 of 5% × stock price. This explains why calls trade above put value by the interest carry amount.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Transaction Costs Affect Choice Between Real and Synthetic
body: Theoretically, real and synthetic positions are equivalent. In practice, transaction costs (bid-ask spreads, commissions) often favor one over the other. Professionals choose whichever form minimizes transaction costs in the current market. The key insight: knowing the synthetic equivalent helps traders evaluate whether they are paying fair value or whether one form is relatively cheaper at any given moment.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Arbitrage: Riskless Profit from Mispricing
body: Arbitrage is buying and selling the same economic exposure in different markets simultaneously to capture a risk-free profit. In options: if put-call parity is violated (actual prices differ from theoretical), traders can lock in profit by constructing the appropriate combination. True arbitrage requires no directional view — all Greeks (delta, gamma, vega, theta) approximately cancel. Used by market makers to maintain pricing efficiency.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: The Conversion: Locking In Riskless Profit
body: Conversion = long stock + long put + short call (same strike, same expiry). Net delta ≈ 0. P/L is the discrepancy between actual market prices and put-call parity. Example: long stock at $100, long 100 Put at $3.50, short 100 Call at $8.25 — if put-call parity says the call should be worth $8.00, the $0.25 mispricing is a riskless $25 profit per contract. Market makers execute conversions to arbitrage away such discrepancies.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: The Reverse Conversion: Mirror of the Conversion
body: Reverse conversion = short stock + short put + long call (same strike, same expiry). Mirror image of conversion. Used when calls are underpriced relative to puts (reverse parity violation). The short stock rebate (interest income from short sale proceeds) significantly affects reverse conversion profitability — professional traders with high rebate rates find more reverse conversions viable than retail traders.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Conversion Pricing Formula: Net Credit Required
body: Conversion target price for the call: Strike + (interest × days/365) + put price − stock price. This formula ensures the net credit received from the conversion exactly equals the interest that could be earned on the strike price capital over the holding period. If the actual call trades above this formula price, a conversion can be profitably executed. The formula is per-share and must be adjusted for actual trade size.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Box Spread: Riskless Instrument Worth (Strike Difference) at Expiration
body: Box spread = bull call spread (buy lower call, sell higher call) + bear put spread (buy higher put, sell lower put), same strikes. At expiration, a 90–100 box is always worth exactly $10 regardless of stock price. Present value = $10 − interest. If the box trades below present value, buying it locks in a risk-free profit equal to the difference. Boxes are pure interest-rate instruments: no directional, gamma, or vega exposure.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Pin Risk in Conversions and Reversals
body: Pin risk arises when stock is exactly at the strike at expiration. The market maker holding a conversion doesn't know if the short call will be exercised. If they hedge assuming no assignment and then receive assignment (or vice versa), they end up with an unexpected large stock position overnight. This is not theoretical — it happens at every expiration when stocks close at or near popular strikes. Professional traders monitor short strikes approaching expiration carefully.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Long Box Spread: Locking In Below-Fair-Value Pricing
body: A 90–100 long box (long 90C, short 100C, short 90P, long 100P) costs net debit at entry. If the box is fairly priced: debit = PV($10) = $10 − interest. If market prices make the box cost less than PV, buying the box locks in a risk-free profit. Example from book: box cost $9.14 against PV of $9.93 → $0.79 profit. Boxes are used by large institutions to lend or borrow at effective interest rates determined by market conditions.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Short Box Spread: Borrowing Against the Spread Value
body: Short box = sell bull call spread + sell bear put spread (same strikes). Receives net credit at entry. At expiration, short box always pays out exactly the spread width. Short box is equivalent to borrowing: you receive cash now, pay back the full spread value later. Cost of borrowing = spread value − net credit received. Market makers use short boxes when borrowing rates in the box market are cheaper than other financing.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Arbitrage Is the Enforcer of Put-Call Parity
body: Put-call parity holds not because of theory but because market makers actively exploit any violation through conversions, reversals, and box spreads. The moment a mispricing appears, professional traders with low transaction costs attack it, driving prices back into alignment. For retail traders: the parity relationship constrains option prices in observable ways, ensuring calls and puts at the same strike reflect the same forward price.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Historical Volatility: Annualized Standard Deviation of Returns
body: Historical volatility (HV) is the annualized standard deviation of daily logarithmic returns over a specified period. Common windows: 30-day, 90-day, 180-day, 300-day HV. Calculation: (1) compute daily returns as ln(today/yesterday); (2) compute standard deviation; (3) annualize by multiplying by √252 (or √256). HV is backward-looking and describes what the stock has done — not what it will do.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Normal Distribution and Expected Stock Price Range
body: Stock returns are approximately normally distributed. The 1σ range around the current price defines the expected range with 68% probability. The 2σ range: 95% probability; 3σ: 99%. Using IV as the volatility input: expected 1-day move = IV / √252 × stock price. Expected 1-year range = ±1σ = ±IV × stock price. This is why a $100 stock at 32% IV has an expected 1-year range of $68–$132 (±1σ).

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Implied Volatility: The Market's Forward Volatility Forecast
body: Implied volatility (IV) is the volatility value that, when plugged into a pricing model with all other known inputs, produces the observed market option price. IV is the market's consensus forecast of future realized volatility over the option's life. Unlike HV (backward-looking), IV is forward-looking. Example from book: Gary calculates theoretical call value at 26% vol = $2.57, but market prices it at $3.40 — implying vol of 32.84%.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: IV Term Structure: How Implied Vol Varies by Expiration
body: IV varies across expiration dates, creating a term structure (or volatility term structure). Normal (contango): longer-dated IV > shorter-dated (uncertainty increases with time). Inverted (backwardation): short-term IV > long-term (event-driven — e.g., earnings approaching). For calendar spreads: buy the back month when it's cheaper than front; sell when it's richer. Term structure shifts are a source of profits and losses for traders holding multi-expiry positions.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Volatility Skew: Why OTM Puts Have Higher IV than OTM Calls
body: Equity option volatility skew: OTM puts have consistently higher implied vol than equidistant OTM calls (downward-sloping IV vs. strike curve). Causes: (1) demand for downside protection (investors buy puts as insurance); (2) asymmetric fear of crashes vs. rallies. Practical implication: a 90-strike put may trade 8+ vol points above a 110-strike call on the same stock. This creates opportunities in risk reversals: sell the rich OTM put, buy the cheap OTM call.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Volatility Can Remain 'Wrong' for Extended Periods
body: Just because IV appears elevated relative to historical vol doesn't mean it will normalize before expiration. IV can remain high for weeks or months if uncertainty persists (earnings cycle, litigation, macro uncertainty). Similarly, IV can stay depressed in calm markets longer than expected. Traders who sell 'expensive' IV face the risk of IV expanding further — especially in markets approaching shock events. Never assume mean reversion is imminent.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Expected vs. Realized vs. Implied Volatility: Three Distinct Concepts
body: Three volatility terms are often confused: (1) Historical/Realized volatility: what the stock has done — backward-looking. (2) Implied volatility: what the market prices in via options — forward-looking, market consensus. (3) Expected volatility: a trader's personal forecast of future realized vol. The vol trade is always a comparison: does the trader's expected vol differ from implied vol? If yes, and if the trader is right, they profit.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Delta-Neutral Trading: Isolating Volatility as the Bet
body: Delta-neutral trading neutralizes directional (stock price) exposure, leaving the position primarily exposed to volatility. Established by: (1) taking an option position (creates delta); (2) trading stock in opposite direction to offset delta. Example: long 20 calls at 50 delta = +1,000 delta → short 1,000 shares → delta-neutral. Remaining exposures: gamma (movement benefit/cost), vega (IV benefit/cost), theta (time decay).

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Long Delta-Neutral: Betting on High Realized Volatility
body: Long delta-neutral = long options + short stock. Profits if realized vol exceeds IV (gamma scalping wins exceed theta paid). Best setup: IV is depressed below historical range; catalyst event approaching. P/L from gamma scalps accumulates as stock oscillates. If stock makes large moves repeatedly, gamma scalps compound into significant profit even while theta erodes the position daily.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Short Delta-Neutral: Betting on Low Realized Volatility
body: Short delta-neutral = short options + long stock. Profits if realized vol is less than IV (theta collected exceeds gamma losses from stock moves). Best setup: IV is elevated above historical range; stock is in a calm, range-bound phase. Theta income accumulates daily. Risk: a sudden large move creates gamma losses that may overwhelm the theta collected. Requires active delta hedging to prevent large directional losses.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Gamma Scalping: Monetizing Realized Volatility
body: Gamma scalping: a long gamma position (long options + short stock delta-neutral) profits by repeatedly rebalancing. As stock rises: delta increases → sell stock to re-neutralize → lock in a small gain. As stock falls: delta decreases → buy stock to re-neutralize → lock in another small gain. Each round-trip scalp generates a small profit. The total of all scalps is gamma P/L. If total scalp profit > theta paid, the long gamma position wins.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Breakeven Condition: When Gamma Scalps Equal Theta
body: Long gamma position breaks even when total gamma scalp profits equal total theta paid. Rule of thumb: the daily realized move must equal approximately the 1-day expected move implied by IV (IV/√252 × stock price). If actual daily moves consistently exceed this threshold → long gamma wins. If actual moves consistently fall short → short gamma (theta collection) wins. This is the fundamental test: will realized vol exceed implied vol?

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Rebalancing Frequency: Transaction Costs vs. Gamma Capture
body: Delta-neutral positions require rebalancing as stock moves (gamma causes delta to drift). Rebalancing too frequently: transaction costs (bid-ask × shares) eat all gamma scalp profits. Rebalancing too rarely: large directional exposure builds up, defeating the purpose of delta neutrality. Professional rule: rebalance when delta drifts by roughly 1 standard deviation of expected stock movement. This balances cost vs. risk.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: IV vs. Realized Vol: The Core Risk of Delta-Neutral Trades
body: The primary risk of delta-neutral trading is that the vol forecast is wrong. Long gamma: if IV collapses and realized vol is low → theta destroys the position faster than gamma scalps recover. Short gamma: if realized vol spikes → gamma losses exceed theta collected. Both sides face the core problem: you are not trading the stock; you are trading the relationship between IV and realized vol. Being wrong on that relationship loses money even if the directional hedge works perfectly.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Speculators vs. Market Makers in Delta-Neutral Trading
body: Two types of delta-neutral traders: (1) Speculators — use IV vs. realized vol forecasts to express a view; assume the risk that their forecast is wrong; hold positions for days to weeks. (2) Market makers — use delta-neutral hedging as a short-term technique to close positions at bid or ask before IV changes adversely; typically hold positions for minutes to hours. Both share the delta-neutral framework but have completely different objectives.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Theory of the Bid-Ask Spread: Market Makers Earn the Edge
body: Market makers earn profit by buying at the bid and selling at the ask. They delta-hedge each trade immediately to neutralize directional risk. Then they attempt to close the hedge at a profit before market conditions change. Example: sell 10 calls at bid 1.85, hedge with +460 shares at 54.03. Stock rises to 55.00. Buy back calls at ask 1.85 — but sell stock at 55.00 → profit from stock move. The bid-ask edge is captured by being the liquidity provider.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Bid-Ask Spread Theory: Risk When Stock Moves Adversely
body: Adverse scenario: buy 10 calls at bid 1.85, hedge with −400 shares at 54.01. Stock falls to 53.00 (adverse). Calls fall to 1.46 (bid). Buy back stock at 53.01, sell calls at 1.46 — the stock gain partially offsets call loss. Net P/L depends on whether the delta hedge captured more than the bid-ask loss on the options. Market makers must close positions before the bid-ask edge is eroded by adverse moves.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Setting Bid and Ask Prices Using Theoretical Value
body: Market makers set bids and asks around their theoretical value (TV). A call with TV = 3.50 might be quoted 3.40–3.60. The market maker will buy at 3.40 (TV − edge) and sell at 3.60 (TV + edge). Edge = bid-ask spread / 2. If the market maker can consistently trade at both bid and ask, profit = 2 × edge per round-trip. Competitors narrow spreads over time — profitable market making requires low transaction costs and efficient hedging.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: National Best Bid and Offer: Customer Price Protection
body: NBBO (National Best Bid and Offer) ensures public traders receive the best available price across all exchanges. Market makers must fill public orders at the NBBO or better. If Exchange A quotes 3.40–3.60 and Exchange B quotes 3.45–3.55, a public order to buy will be filled at 3.55 (the lowest ask). This protects public traders but forces market makers to compete aggressively on pricing.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Reverse Conversion Pricing: Calculating Target Call Price
body: Reverse conversion target call price = stock price − put price + (interest × days/365). If stock = 55, put = 1.50, interest = 4%, 30 days: target call = 55 − 1.50 + 0.18 = 53.68. If market call is below this, a profitable reverse conversion is possible. The formula tells the market maker exactly what price they need for the call to lock in the target profit. Deviations from this price = arbitrage opportunity.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Box Spread Pricing in Practice: Locking In Interest Rate Returns
body: Box spread present value = (high strike − low strike) × [1 − (interest × days/365)]. A 90–100 box with 60 days and 4% interest: PV = 10 × [1 − (0.04 × 60/365)] = 10 × 0.9934 = 9.93. If the box can be purchased for $9.14, the locked-in profit is $0.79 per share — equivalent to lending at a rate higher than 4%. Institutional traders use box spreads as synthetic money market instruments when rates are favorable.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Two-Trade Arbitrage: Creating Conversions Across Exchanges
body: Conversions can be executed in two separate trades to capture edge. Trade 1: buy stock + sell call (or buy put). Trade 2: complete the other leg. By splitting the trade, the market maker can capture the bid-ask spread on each leg separately. Total profit = sum of edges on each component minus transaction costs. This requires speed and execution precision — the opportunity closes as prices adjust.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Chapter 10: Managing Position Risk — Overview
body: Position risk management for a multi-option portfolio requires: (1) computing position Greeks (delta, gamma, vega, theta, rho) across all positions; (2) understanding how these Greeks change as market conditions change; (3) identifying which Greek creates the most risk; (4) setting risk limits for each Greek; (5) hedging Greeks that exceed limits. Traders must understand how position Greeks evolve — not just their current values.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Bull Call Spread Position Risk: How Greeks Evolve
body: For 20 long 70–75 call spreads: (1) Position value peaks between strikes. (2) Delta peaks when stock is between strikes (both options ATM-ish). (3) Gamma is positive below lower strike (long call dominates), negative above upper strike (short call dominates), zero between. (4) Vega positive between strikes, near zero outside. (5) Theta mirrors vega — most negative between strikes. Understanding these dynamics prevents surprises when the stock moves into or out of the spread range.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Setting Risk Limits Based on Position Greeks
body: Risk limits should be set in dollar terms for each Greek: max delta exposure (directional risk), max gamma (move risk), max vega (IV risk), max theta (time cost). Example: if position delta is $5,268, a $1 adverse move costs $5,268. If maximum acceptable daily loss is $10,000, the position is at risk from a ~2-point adverse move. Greeks translate directly into dollar risk limits, enabling objective stop-loss decision making.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Neutralizing Greeks: When and Why
body: Any Greek can be neutralized by taking an offsetting position. To neutralize delta: trade stock. To neutralize gamma and vega: trade options (only options change gamma and vega significantly). To neutralize theta: it follows from gamma/vega neutrality. Traders choose which Greek to emphasize: a speculative vol bet keeps vega exposure large; a market-neutral position minimizes all Greeks. The goal of neutralization is to eliminate unintended risk while retaining the desired exposure.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Position Theta and the Rho-Theta Link with Interest Rates
body: When interest rates are zero: neutralizing gamma also neutralizes theta and vega (they move together). When rates are non-zero: theta also includes an interest-rate component (cost of carry), so neutralizing gamma does not fully neutralize theta. The interest component of theta is linked to rho. For high-rate environments or long-dated positions, carry costs become a meaningful part of daily P/L and must be tracked separately.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Greeks Are Snapshots, Not Constants
body: Position Greeks change as market conditions change. A position with delta = +500 today may have delta = +800 if the stock rises $5 (gamma effect). Vega may shrink as time passes. Theta may accelerate as expiration approaches. Traders who rely on static Greek calculations — without understanding how they will evolve — will be surprised. The graphs of position Greeks vs. stock price (Ch. 10 figures) illustrate how entire risk profiles shift dynamically.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Bull Call Spread: Delta, Gamma, Vega, Theta at Three Time Horizons
body: 20 long 70–75 call spreads at three time horizons (expiration, 35 days, 17 days): Delta: peaks ~1,800 between strikes; zero outside. Gamma: positive below $70, negative above $75 (zero crossing between strikes). Vega: bell-shaped positive (max between strikes). Theta: mirror of vega — most negative between strikes. All four Greeks are highest in magnitude when stock is between the strikes — the position's 'hot zone.'

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Position Greeks Table: Calculating Spread Greeks from Components
body: 70–75 call spread Greeks: 70 Call at delta 0.535, gamma 0.059, vega 0.087, theta −0.310. Minus 75 Call: delta 0.262, gamma 0.049, vega 0.066, theta −0.225. Net per spread: delta 0.273, gamma 0.010, vega 0.021, theta +0.085. Multiplied by 100 × 20 contracts: position delta = 546, gamma = 20, vega = 42, theta = 170 (daily income). Each Greek is additive across legs — the position's total Greek exposure equals the sum of all component legs.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Identifying the Key Risk Greek for a Position
body: Different positions have different primary risks: long call spread → vega risk (IV change between strikes); short straddle → gamma risk (large moves) and vega risk (IV spike); covered call → delta risk with secondary theta benefit. Bittman advises identifying the one Greek that most threatens the position under adverse scenarios, then either hedging it or setting a dollar-denominated limit for it. This focuses risk management on what matters most.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Three-Part Risk Analysis: Best Case, Worst Case, Most Likely
body: Before entering any position, analyze three scenarios: (1) Best case — forecast correct, IV favorable, time passes: what is the maximum profit? (2) Worst case — forecast wrong, IV adverse, time passes: what is the maximum loss? (3) Most likely case — stock moves moderately, IV stays roughly constant: what is the expected P/L? This three-part analysis determines if the risk-reward is acceptable and where to place stop-losses.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Position Greeks Change Direction as Stock Crosses Strike
body: A bull call spread's gamma changes sign as the stock crosses the short-call strike. Below the lower strike: positive gamma (benefits from moves). Above the upper strike: negative gamma (hurts from moves). Traders who don't recognize this flip can be surprised when their 'long gamma' spread suddenly becomes 'short gamma' after a big move. Always re-evaluate Greeks whenever stock moves significantly relative to strikes.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Greek Neutralization Strategy: Choosing Which Greek to Keep
body: A trader can selectively neutralize Greeks they don't want while keeping those they do. Example: want to bet on IV rising (keep long vega) but not on direction (neutralize delta with stock) and not on gamma (add offsetting options to reduce gamma). This selective Greek management is how sophisticated traders isolate specific risk factors. The cost of neutralizing unwanted Greeks is the transaction cost of the hedging trades.

book_title: My Learnings   Trading Options As A Professional
author: James B. Bittman
title: Understanding Greeks Combination — The Professional Edge
body: Bittman's concluding principle: professionals who understand how all five Greeks interact — not just individually — have a decisive edge. A position can look safe on delta but dangerous on gamma; safe on theta but exposed on vega. Only by evaluating the full Greek profile across realistic market scenarios does a trader truly understand what they own. The Greeks are a language for describing risk; fluency in that language is the mark of a professional.
